title: Someone Who Got There First
description:
An investment seminar. The presenter stepped up.

"Hi, I'm Lee Minseo. I started in a Gangnam jeonse apartment [rented deposit-only] at 35, and now I own the place outright. I'm 38."

[Jeonse: Korea's unique deposit-only rental system. Instead of monthly rent, you pay a large lump-sum (often 100 million won-500M+) that sits with the landlord. No monthly payments. At lease end, you get the full deposit back. It's how many Koreans 'step into' expensive areas without buying.]

Started at 35. Goal reached at 38. Three years.

{name} ran the numbers. That timeline is almost identical to his.

choices.text: Get her business card after the talk — want to ask how
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo smiled and handed over her card.

A handshake with someone who owns a Gangnam apartment. Slightly unreal. And — she was once standing where {name} is standing.

choices.text: Just listened and left — no nerve to approach
choices.result_text:
On the way home, her words kept running through his head.

Not 'it can be done' — but 'she already did it.' That stayed longer than expected.

title: Beyond Gangnam
description:
Ran into Lee Minseo at a café near the seminar venue. Different face than on stage.

"Oh — you were at the seminar, weren't you?"

Coffee together. She said things she didn't say at the talk.

"Honestly — I got more exhausted after buying the apartment. There's the mortgage. Kids' tutoring costs. And even though the price went up, I can't sell — I live there."

Got Gangnam — and Gangnam got her.

choices.text: "But you achieved the goal." — see the positive
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo smiled briefly. "Yes. I did achieve it."

But that smile was different somehow. {name} wanted to understand the difference. Probably have to get there to know.

choices.text: "Is there something I'm not seeing? Tell me honestly." — ask directly
choices.result_text:
She thought for a moment, then said:
"When you have a goal — you have to be ready for when the goal disappears. That's the hardest part."

It took {name} a while to understand what that meant.

title: The One Who Arrives
description:
Gangnam wasn't far now.

With the number nearly full, a message came from Lee Minseo.
"I heard. They say you're almost there."

They met again at that same cafe.
"Congratulations. I mean it."
Then she went quiet for a moment.
"Remember what I told you back then?"

{name} remembered. 'When you have a goal, prepare for when it disappears.'
Now — he was starting to understand what she meant.

choices.text: "I think I'm starting to get it." — said it honestly
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo nodded.
"Right? When you arrive, the next question comes. 'So now what.'
But that's not all bad. At least — it's a new question."

For the first time, {name} felt that Gangnam wasn't the end, but the start of the next sentence.

choices.text: "I haven't arrived yet. Don't want to count my chickens." — smiled
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo laughed. "Fair enough. See it all the way through."

Still, {name} decided to tuck her words away in his bag.
He'd take them out once he got there.

It was Minjun who had reached out first, using that business card.
Not because he had a question — because he needed someone to ask.

People who have thought about it and people who haven't — they look at different things from the same finish line.

title: Even If You Don't Arrive
description:
Gangnam was still far off. The number hadn't filled.

And then Minseo reached out.
"How are you holding up? Almost there?"

Minjun answered honestly. Still far. Maybe he wouldn't make it at all.

Minseo was quiet a moment, then said,
"Remember what I told you? To prepare for when the goal disappears."
"...Yeah."
"Here's the thing — even if you don't reach the goal, you need that same preparation. The one who arrives and the one who doesn't. In the end the question left over is the same."
"What question?"
"Whether that goal was ever really yours."

choices.text: "It was mine. It still is."
choices.result_text:
Minseo smiled.
"Then you're fine. Arriving is a separate problem."

He hung up and looked out the window. Gangnam was still far away.
But strangely — today the distance didn't ache the way it used to.

choices.text: "I don't know. Not anymore."
choices.result_text:
Minseo didn't scold the answer.
"Asking that even now — that puts you ahead of the ones who arrived."

Minjun held the phone for a long time.
Even if he never reached Gangnam, what he shouldn't lose along the way — he was starting to understand it, a little.

title: The Cost Sheet After Arrival
description:
At 11:30 Saturday morning, Minseo entered the cafe near the seminar at the time {name} had arranged. In {name}'s bag, the R4-SELF contract and the clinic copy from the previous day shared one clear folder. Minseo offered neither congratulations nor consolation. She turned her calculator facedown and asked,

“The contract has a loss cap. How much of your day can you lose before you stop?”

{name} began to explain whether he had reached the goal, then closed his mouth. Minseo drew three boxes on a napkin—money, body, people—and pushed it over while they were still blank. “Not your balance. Write one price you've already paid.” As the foam sank in his coffee, {name} chose one box he could no longer keep hidden.

texts: Inside the clear folder, the doctor's marks on the fourteen-day record and the circles around nights below four hours remained beneath the clinic stamp. Minseo saw the folded copy and pushed the calculator farther away.

The phone held three hand-tremor videos with different timestamps, while the meal and caffeine fields on the clinic form remained unanswered. Minseo had {name} place the screen on the table with those blanks visible too.

Two colors on the clinic copy divided work past midnight from missed meals and failed to skip a single one of four weeks. Minseo opened that schedule beside the napkin before asking about the hidden amounts.

choices.text: Place the clinic evidence that first made the body's cost visible in the body box
choices.result_text:
{name} opened the clinic copy from the previous day and turned the observation material marked by the doctor toward Minseo. She entered neither its figures nor its times into the calculator.

“That's principal, not yield. If the principal is wearing away while you count only returns, the ledger is lying.”

{name} folded the clinic copy again. The crease ran through the body box, leaving only what the clinic had actually observed on the sheet.

choices.text: Place the R4-SELF he had opened with Daeun in the people box, turned to the weekend-and-night clause
choices.result_text:
{name} took out the R4-SELF he had opened with Daeun and set it down with the weekend-and-night clause visible. Minseo read the sentence containing those two words slowly.

“That's not time spent on a person. It's a contract spending the time that belonged to one. Those use different arithmetic.”

Minseo did not say Daeun's name aloud. The cafe light narrowed over the words weekend and night.

choices.text: Write R3's 70 million won additional-funding figure in the money box
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote R3's 70 million won additional-funding figure in the money box and added the Friday deadline. Minseo asked, “When you fill that figure, what goes in the next blank?”

{name} had no immediate answer. Minseo left the napkin open beneath her cup. Only the money box was dark with ink; the body and people boxes remained empty at the edge of the coffee ring.

title: The Sheet Before a Diagnosis
description:
At 9:20 Friday morning, {name} sat in the family-medicine exam room he had booked. On the desk lay fourteen days of sleep records, a blank form for the times his hand trembled, and a blood-pressure slip. The doctor looked at {name}'s hands before the monitor and capped the pen.

“I won't name this from one screen. Choose the information we must not leave out: sleep, tremors, or the hours you worked.”

A registration band was already fastened around {name}'s wrist. He had to slide one set of records across without hiding it. A queue number sounded once in the corridor, and fluorescent light spread over the still-empty diagnosis field.

texts: Daeun's blue line under 420 million won showed through the clear folder on the exam-room chair. When {name} moved to cover that page, the doctor looked at his hand before the screen.

{name} remembered Daeun's finger tracing the days between R3's authoring time and the name-removal request. Until his queue number sounded, he matched those days against the dates in his sleep and tremor records.

Daeun's blue vertical line still split NIGHT from PRIORITY in the weekend-and-night clause. As {name} put that page into the folder, the schedule of hours actually worked past midnight showed directly behind it.

choices.text: Hand over all fourteen days of sleep records with the dates visible
choices.result_text:
{name} handed over all fourteen days instead of selecting only the nights he slept well. The doctor circled the nights below four hours and left a field beside them for follow-up.

No diagnosis was added. The stamped copy held only dense rows of sleep and waking times. {name} folded it in half and placed it in the clear folder.

choices.text: Show the hand-tremor videos with their timestamps
choices.result_text:
{name} played three videos of his hand trembling around a water bottle, keeping each timestamp visible. The doctor paused the images to ask about caffeine and meal intervals, leaving unanswered fields blank.

Instead of a confirmed name, three observation times entered the form. When the phone went dark, a steady hand appeared briefly in the black glass.

choices.text: Open the contract calendar and the hours actually worked
choices.result_text:
{name} hid the income figures and contract names, then showed the start and finish times from the last four weeks. The doctor marked the blocks past midnight and the missing meals in different colors.

“You don't have to discuss the money. We do need the hours your body worked.”

The clinic copy held time without amounts. Neither color skipped a single week.

title: Not Whatever Day Is Left
description:
At 7:40 Sunday evening, {name} unfolded the napkin on which Minseo had drawn three boxes. Only the box he had chosen before Minseo held one trace—a figure, the folded clinic copy, or the open weekend-and-night clause; the other two remained blank. Pressing the space between the three boxes with one finger, {name} asked,

“After three billion won, what kind of day should we still protect together?”

Daeun did not answer at once. She turned her phone facedown and pulled the weekend-and-night clause from R4-SELF beside the napkin.

“Minjun, don't give me time left after you've counted all the money. Tell me what time is mine from the beginning. Then I'll tell you what I would give up for it.”

The question had already been asked. {name} had to take one real boundary from the calendar.

texts: The body box held the crease left by the clinic copy. When {name} repeated Minseo's word for that evidence—principal—Daeun asked whether this promise would spend the body as another cost.
R4-SELF lay open over the people box. When {name} repeated Minseo's warning that the contract was spending time that belonged to a person, Daeun refused to call that time whatever remained for her.
Only R3's 70 million won additional-funding figure and the Friday deadline darkened the money box; body and people stayed blank. Daeun pointed to both empty boxes before she opened the calendar.

choices.text: Say one evening a week will take no contract calls
choices.result_text:
{name} pointed to one Thursday evening. Daeun did not begin by believing the word every.

“Leave this Thursday open first. If you don't keep it, don't stop at saying you were busy. Tell me what you chose instead.”

{name} drew a slash through the contract-alert block after seven. No number showed the money lost, but two hours that could not be sold appeared on the calendar for the first time.

choices.text: Say one Sunday a month will be blocked first, not left over
choices.result_text:
{name} circled the first Sunday of the next month. Daeun opened her schedule to the same date but did not mark the promise complete.

“I don't want a day you meet me because it happened to remain. If you leave it open first, I'll check what I would have to clear that day too.”

The same date glowed on both screens. Daeun set her phone facedown beside the napkin instead of marking anything complete.

choices.text: Say a call about health or family will stop the calculation first
choices.result_text:
{name} drew one line between the clinic form and the family-call entry. Daeun did not nod; she wrote ‘tell me before’ in the people box.

“Explaining after you collapse isn't protecting something together. Let me know before you stop too.”

Neither of them folded the paper until the blue ink dried. The calculator screen went dark first.

title: An Evening That Cannot Be Returned
description:
At 11:30 Saturday morning, Minseo set a thirty-minute alarm at the cafe. She had made time on her way to pick up her child. When {name} opened the appointment proposal, she read the 450,000 won monthly allowance and six-million-won training repayment once, then covered it.

“When I was reaching Gangnam, I counted only money. The first thing I lost was walking home with my child. Buying the apartment later didn't return that time.” Hearing that {name} would meet Hyunsu tomorrow, Minseo looked at the empty chair.

“Name one evening that will remain after the title disappears in twelve months. Not time the company permits. Time you will personally refuse to surrender.” Twenty-two minutes remained. Protecting one person's time meant losing another's expectation or authority.

choices.text: Call the team lead and say one weekday evening is not available to the job
choices.result_text:
Without leaving the cafe, {name} called the team lead. “Wednesday evenings are outside the team schedule. If that's the condition, choose another lead.”

The team lead stayed quiet for a long time, then said he needed someone who would give that time too. The appointment would be reconsidered Monday. Minseo did not praise him. “Now you also have to keep whoever belongs in that evening.” The first proposal remained with {name}; the team lead's expectation cooled, and this week's answer window remained with the company.

choices.text: Tell Minseo to leave on time and carry this decision alone
choices.result_text:
Before Minseo's alarm could ring, {name} put the proposal in his bag. “Go. I won't ask you to make today's answer for me.”

Minseo stood. “If you can choose when I'm absent, {name}, that is your life. Just don't use ‘I chose alone’ as an excuse later.” She called her child as she left the cafe. Her evening was protected, but {name} still had not named the time he would keep from the company. The empty chair and his coffee, not yet cold, waited for that answer.

choices.text: Leave with Minseo and call Hyunsu to promise he will arrive first tomorrow
choices.result_text:
{name} stood with Minseo before her alarm. Outside the cafe, he called Hyunsu and said he would already be at the soup shop when Hyunsu arrived tomorrow.

Hyunsu paused. “Getting there first isn't the answer, hyung. You need something to ask first.” When the call ended, Minseo walked toward her waiting child. {name} looked at the bus stop toward the office in the opposite direction and did not go. He had given up more advice today and the team lead's recommendation for the week, but tomorrow he could arrive before one person's evening was spent waiting for him.

title: What to Ask Before a Name
description:
At 8:05 Sunday evening, in the soup shop by their old goshiwon, {name} left the first proposal in his bag. He set down his phone. “When I saw the external reviewer field, your name came to mind. I didn't use it, and I told the company not to.”

Hyunsu set down his spoon and waited for the steam to sink. “Hyung, before you say you didn't use it, tell me why you needed my name.” {name} explained how an outside name cut approval from fifteen business days to five. Hyunsu kept looking at those ten days.

“Then what will you protect after the appointment? In your life, not in my name.”

{name} kept his calendar closed and looked between Hyunsu's work schedule, water glass, and overturned phone. One question about how Hyunsu protected his work stayed in his mouth—the hardest to ask now.

choices.text: Ask how he protects an evening he will not sell to the office
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu opened his work schedule and pointed to one block from the previous month. “I don't protect a day perfectly. But when I lose an evening, I don't pretend I repaid it by spending next week's time on someone.”

When {name} asked, “Then what about me?” Hyunsu closed the screen. “You have to clear your own calendar, hyung.”

The shape of one empty evening remained between the bowls. Hyunsu's hand stopped beside his water glass instead of reaching for {name}'s calendar.

choices.text: Ask how he survives without putting his name on figures he could not verify
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu wiped a ring of water from the rim of his glass. “I don't put my name on figures I couldn't verify, even if it means I don't get the assignment. But I explain the part I did verify to the end.”

“Would you have refused this one too?”

“If you'd asked me first.” Hyunsu's answer was short. The unasked time remained on the table longer than the name he had not used.

choices.text: Ask how not to turn a person into collateral on a day money is tight
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu turned the water glass half a circle, then pointed at {name}'s phone. “Don't send the request first. Send the situation: how much is urgent, why it's me, and whether there's room for me to say no.”

After a moment, he added, “And don't ask me to write the refusal for you too.”

Only the ceiling light reflected in the black phone screen. One sentence that would have made Hyunsu supervise the boundary was erased before it entered the field.

title: A Lunch Going Cold
description: Months later, {name} met Minseo for a late lunch and spoke about the acquisition that still had not ended. He said KRW 3.2 billion would reach a goal he had chased for years, but she did not check the arithmetic for him. Then Sujin called. When {name} said Minseo was there, Sujin paused and gave permission first: “It's okay if I'm on speaker.” She asked only, “I don't care what the company is called, but it will still work Monday, right?” Minseo looked at the cooling soup. “KRW 3.2 billion is the goal, you said. Who is giving up time to answer this call today?” She made clear she would not supply the legal or personal answer. As their lunch time ended, the acquirer called too.

choices.text: End lunch early and keep listening to Sujin before answering the acquirer
choices.result_text:
{name} silenced the acquirer's call and asked which part of Monday frightened Sujin most. She said they would know only after logging in that morning and did not press him for a guarantee. Minseo paid for her untouched food and picked up her bag.

“I didn't choose today's answer,” she said before leaving. Their lunch and her time would not return, and Sujin's worry had not vanished after one call. {name} sent the co-founder a short message asking to meet again that night.

title: The Night the Coats Came Off Again
description: That night, just as the last teammate reached the door with a bag, Sujin called again. “It worked earlier, but it stopped again.” The co-founder froze halfway through zipping a coat and looked at {name}. An important meeting with the acquirer waited the next morning, and this was the only night the founders could prepare together. The co-founder nodded toward the people at the door. “If you stay, it costs your sleep. If we both go, we lose our only time to talk alone. If you stay in the meeting room, those people have to take their coats off again.” Sujin would see whose night kept the service alive. No one could promise the failure would end.

choices.text: Take the night support alone and send the co-founder and team home
choices.result_text:
{name} told the co-founder to zip the coat and told the team not to return. Alone, he followed Sujin's screen past midnight and watched the same failure appear once more. “You're still there,” she said, but she did not say everything was fine.

The questions the co-founder had left for tomorrow stayed unopened. {name}'s sleep and preparation time passed into the customer's night, and he never promised it would be solved by morning.

choices.text: Go to Sujin together and send the whole team home
choices.result_text:
{name} and the co-founder sent the team home and went to Sujin. The acquirer kept asking for material for tomorrow, but neither opened a laptop on the way. Seeing the same failure beside Sujin made only one thing clearer: it did not have a single cause.

They protected the team's night, but lost both their preparation and the last private hours in which the two founders could speak about what would come if the company changed hands. Only the customer's words remained on the trip back.

choices.text: Prepare for the acquirer while the co-founder and team take the night
choices.result_text:
{name} stayed in the meeting room while the co-founder and team took off their coats again. Short questions and keyboards carried through the call with Sujin all night. {name} prepared what he would say to the acquirer and learned only in the morning what else had happened to the customer.

On the next call, Sujin said the co-founder's name and the team's names first. The acquisition preparation survived, and so did the memory of {name}'s absence. The cost of holding the failure came out of other people's sleep.
